1F (Linear Algebra)

Words: 109 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 109
1F OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form B on V is nondegenerate when
B(v,w)=0for every v∈V⟹w=0.
(1)
In finite dimensions this is equivalent to nondegeneracy in the first argument.
Define the linear map
β1​:V⟶V∗,β1​(w)=B1​(−,w).
(2)
Nondegeneracy makes β1​ injective. Since V and its dual space have the same finite dimension, β1​ is an isomorphism. Similarly define β2​(w)=B2​(−,w) and set
α=β1−1​β2​​.
(3)
Then α is linear and
B1​(v,αw)=β1​(αw)(v)=β2​(w)(v)=B2​(v,w).
(4)
If w∈kerα, this identity gives B2​(v,w)=0 for every v. Conversely, if B2​(v,w)=0 for every v, then B1​(v,αw)=0 for every v, so nondegeneracy gives αw=0. Hence
{w∈V:B2​(v,w)=0 for every v∈V}=kerα​.
(5)
This is the representation of a bilinear form relative to a nondegenerate bilinear form.

Words: 140
2G OurBigBook.com
Fix x∈X. By assumption there is a neighbourhood U of x on which fn​→f with uniform convergence. Each restriction fn​∣U​ is continuous, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. Thus f∣U​ is continuous, in particular at x. Since x was arbitrary, f is continuous on X.
Now let K⊆X be compact and let ε>0. For each x∈K, choose a neighbourhood Ux​ on which convergence is uniform. The sets Ux​ cover K, so compactness gives a finite subcover
K⊆Ux1​​∪⋯∪Uxm​​.
(6)
For each j, choose Nj​ such that
n≥Nj​, y∈Uxj​​⟹∣fn​(y)−f(y)∣<ε.
(7)
Taking N=maxj​Nj​, every y∈K belongs to one of these finitely many neighbourhoods, and therefore
n≥N⟹supy∈K​∣fn​(y)−f(y)∣<ε.
(8)
Thus fn​→f uniformly on every compact subset. This proves the local uniform convergence on compact subsets principle.

i OurBigBook.com
The domains are not conformally equivalent. Suppose that F:C∖{0}→{w:0<∣w∣<1} were a conformal equivalence. Since F is bounded near zero, the Riemann removable singularity theorem extends it holomorphically across zero. The extension is a bounded entire function, so the Liouville theorem makes it constant, contradicting bijectivity. This is the punctured plane is not conformally equivalent to the punctured unit disc obstruction.

The domains are not conformally equivalent. If F:C→H were a conformal equivalence, composing it with a Cayley transform from the upper half-plane H to the unit disc would produce a bounded nonconstant entire function. This contradicts the Liouville theorem, proving that the complex plane is not conformally equivalent to the upper half-plane.

T(z)=1−z1+z​

F(z)=(1−z1+z​)2​
(10)
is the required equivalence, as recorded by the conformal equivalence between the upper half-disc and upper half-plane.

For a particle in the scalar potential energy U(x),
H=2mp2​+U(x).
(15)
The canonical commutation relation [x,p]=iℏ gives
[H,x]=2m1​[p2,x]=−miℏ​p.
(16)
The Ehrenfest theorem with O=x therefore gives
mdtd​⟨x⟩ψ​=⟨p⟩ψ​​.
(17)
Since [p2,p]=0 and direct action on a wavefunction gives [U(x),p]=iℏU′(x),
dtd​⟨p⟩ψ​=−⟨U′(x)⟩ψ​​.
(18)
Finally H has no explicit time dependence and [H,H]=0, so
dtd​⟨H⟩ψ​=0​.
(19)
The first two equations are the expectation-value counterparts of momentum equals mass times velocity and Newton's second law; the last is conservation of energy. They become the classical equations directly when the force varies negligibly across the wave packet, so that ⟨U′(x)⟩≃U′(⟨x⟩). These conclusions are summarized by the classical equations from Ehrenfest theorem.

Φ(r)=4πϵ0​Q​(rN​−∣r−dz∣1​−∣r+dz∣M​).

∣r∓dz∣1​=r1​[1±rd​cosθ+2r2d2​(3cos2θ−1)+O(r−3)].

Φ(r,θ)=4πϵ0​Q​[rN−M−1​+r2(M−1)dcosθ​−2r3(M+1)d2(3cos2θ−1)​+O(r−4)]​.

The three displayed terms are respectively the monopole, dipole, and quadrupole terms of the electric multipole expansion. In particular, the total charge is Q(N−M−1) and the electric dipole moment is Qd(M−1)z. This is the multipole expansion of three collinear charges.

The nonzero orthogonal polynomials Q0​,…,Qn​ have distinct degrees and form an orthogonal basis of Pn​. Define
pn∗​=∑k=0n​⟨Qk​,Qk​⟩⟨f,Qk​⟩​Qk​.
(29)
For each j≤n,
⟨f−pn∗​,Qj​⟩=⟨f,Qj​⟩−⟨Qj​,Qj​⟩⟨f,Qj​⟩​⟨Qj​,Qj​⟩=0.
(30)
Thus the residual f−pn∗​ is orthogonal to all of Pn​.
For any p∈Pn​, write
f−p=(f−pn∗​)+(pn∗​−p).
(31)
The two terms are orthogonal, so the Pythagorean theorem in an inner-product space gives
∥f−p∥2=∥f−pn∗​∥2+∥pn∗​−p∥2≥∥f−pn∗​∥2.
(32)
Equality holds only for p=pn∗​. This proves the formula and uniqueness of the least-squares polynomial in an orthogonal-polynomial basis.

For ordered bases B=(v1​,…,vn​) of V and C=(w1​,…,wm​) of W, the matrix representation of a linear map γ:V→W is the matrix whose jth column consists of the C-coordinates of γ(vj​). Thus
[γ(v)]C​=[γ]C←B​[v]B​.
(44)
The operators α,β:V→V are conjugate linear operators when there is an isomorphism s:V→V such that
β=s−1αs.
(45)
In one basis their matrices therefore satisfy [β]=[s]−1[α][s], so they are similar matrices.
For invertible β, the map
ϕβ​(A)=β−1Aβ
(46)
is linear, and its inverse is A↦βAβ−1; hence it is a linear isomorphism of End(V). If β′=s−1βs, define Φs​(A)=s−1As. A direct substitution gives
ϕβ′​=Φs​ϕβ​Φs−1​,
(47)
so ϕβ′​ and ϕβ​ are conjugate. This is the conjugation operator on an endomorphism space.
It remains to compute the Jordan normal form over C. By the preceding conjugacy, we may put β in Jordan form.
If
β=(λ0​0μ​),λμ=0,
(48)
then the matrix units Eij​ are eigenvectors because
ϕβ​(Eij​)=βi​βj​​Eij​.
(49)
Thus
JNF(ϕβ​)=diag(1,1,λμ​,μλ​)​.
(50)
This includes the scalar case λ=μ, when ϕβ​ is the identity.
Otherwise β has one size-two Jordan block. Multiplying β by a nonzero scalar does not change ϕβ​, and conjugating within its Jordan class allows us to use J=I+N with N=E12​. Put D=ϕJ​−I. Direct multiplication gives
D(E11​)=E12​,D(E12​)=0,D(E22​)=−E12​,
(51)
D(E21​)=E22​−E11​−E12​.
(52)
Hence D3=0, rankD=2, and rankD2=1. The nilpotent Jordan blocks of D therefore have sizes three and one. Adding the identity gives
JNF(ϕβ​)=J3​(1)⊕J1​(1)​.
(53)

Let
F(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a1​X+a0​∈Z[X]
(54)
be primitive. The Eisenstein criterion states that if a prime number p satisfies
p∤an​,qquadp∣aj​ (0≤j<n),qquadp2∤a0​,
(55)
then F is an irreducible polynomial in Z[X], equivalently in Q[X] by Gauss lemma for polynomials.
To prove it, suppose that F=GH with G,H∈Z[X] of positive degree. Primitivity and Gauss's lemma let us take such an integral factorisation if a factorisation over Q exists. Reducing modulo p gives
GH=an​​Xn.
(56)
Because p does not divide the leading coefficient of F, neither factor loses degree on reduction. The polynomial ring Fp​[X] is a unique factorization domain, so both reductions are monomials of positive degree. In particular, p divides both constant terms G(0) and H(0). It follows that p2 divides
F(0)=G(0)H(0)=a0​,
(57)
a contradiction. This proves the criterion.
For a prime p, translate the geometric sum by one:
f(X+1)=X(X+1)p−1​=∑k=1p​(kp​)Xk−1.
(58)
Its leading coefficient is one, every other coefficient is divisible by p, and its constant coefficient is p, which is not divisible by p2. It is therefore Eisenstein at p. Translation X↦X+1 is an automorphism of Z[X], so
f(X)=1+X+⋯+Xp−1 is irreducible.​
(59)
This is the geometric-sum irreducibility criterion.
The evaluation homomorphism
evζ​:Z[X]⟶C,G⟼G(ζ),
(60)
has image Z[ζ] and contains (f) in its kernel. Since f is monic, division by f in Z[X] writes every G as G=Qf+R with degR<degf. If G(ζ)=0, then R(ζ)=0; the irreducibility of f says that f is the minimal polynomial of ζ, so R=0. Thus ker(evζ​)=(f), and the first isomorphism theorem for rings gives
Z[ζ]≅Z[X]/(f)​.
(61)
Now take p=3. Then ζ2+ζ+1=0, and the Eisenstein integers are
Z[ζ]={a+bζ:a,b∈Z}.
(62)
Complex conjugation sends ζ to ζ2, so the field norm is
N(a+bζ)=(a+bζ)(a+bζ2)=a2−ab+b2=∣a+bζ∣2.
(63)
Given z=x+yζ∈C, choose integers m,n with ∣x−m∣,∣y−n∣≤21​. For q=m+nζ,
∣z−q∣2=(x−m)2−(x−m)(y−n)+(y−n)2≤43​<1.
(64)
For α,β∈Z[ζ] with β=0, apply this to z=α/β and put r=α−qβ. Then
N(r)=N(β)∣z−q∣2<N(β).
(65)
Hence the norm is a Euclidean function, proving that Z[ζ] is a Euclidean domain. This is the Euclidean norm on the Eisenstein integers.
Finally suppose A∈GLn​(Z) satisfies A2+A+I=0. Make the free abelian group M=Zn into a Z[ζ]-module by defining
ζv=Av.
(66)
This is well-defined precisely because A obeys the same polynomial relation as ζ. The module is finitely generated. It is also torsion-free module: if 0=α∈Z[ζ] and αv=0, multiplication by the conjugate of α gives N(α)v=0, and the additive group Zn has no nonzero integer torsion.
A Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain, and the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain says that a finitely generated torsion-free module over one is free. Thus
M≅Z[ζ]m
(67)
for some m. Since Z[ζ] has free module basis 1,ζ over Z, comparison of abelian ranks gives n=2m. There can consequently be no such matrix when n is odd.
If n=2m, choose a Z[ζ]-basis v1​,…,vm​. Then
v1​,Av1​,…,vm​,Avm​
(68)
is a Z-basis, and A2vi​=−vi​−Avi​. In this basis the matrix of A is a direct sum of m copies of
C=(01​−1−1​).
(69)
Every admissible matrix is therefore conjugate in GLn​(Z) to C⊕m. Hence there is exactly one conjugacy class for even n, and none for odd n. This is the classification of integral matrices satisfying the third cyclotomic polynomial.

i OurBigBook.com
A compact space is a topological space in which every open cover has a finite subcover. A Hausdorff space is one in which every two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods. A homeomorphism is a bijection that is continuous and whose inverse is continuous.
For an equivalence relation R on X, let X/R be the set of equivalence classes and let
q:X⟶X/R,q(x)=[x].
(70)
The quotient topology declares U⊆X/R open exactly when q−1(U) is open in X. It follows directly from the definition that q is continuous.
Suppose that the continuous map f:X→Y is constant on equivalence classes. The only possible factorisation is
F:X/R⟶Y,F([x])=f(x),
(71)
which is well-defined by the hypothesis and satisfies F∘q=f. For every open V⊆Y,
q−1(F−1(V))=f−1(V)
(72)
is open in X. The definition of the quotient topology therefore makes F−1(V) open, so F is continuous. This proves the universal property of the quotient topology.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

ii

Words: 218 Articles: 1
10G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 218
ii OurBigBook.com
Let X be compact and q:X→X/R the quotient map. If (Ui​)i∈I​ is an open cover of X/R, then (q−1(Ui​))i∈I​ is an open cover of X. A finite subfamily covers X; because q is surjective, the corresponding Ui​ cover X/R. Thus every quotient of a compact space is compact.
The Hausdorff property need not survive. On the real line, define
xRy⟺x−y∈Q.
(73)
The quotient R/Q has more than one point. If two nonempty open subsets of the quotient were disjoint, their inverse images would be disjoint nonempty open subsets of R invariant under rational translation. But any two nonempty open intervals acquire an intersection after one is translated by a suitably chosen rational number, so two such saturated open sets cannot be disjoint. Distinct quotient points cannot be separated, and the quotient is not Hausdorff. This is the non-Hausdorff quotient of the real line by rational translation.
Finally let f:X→Y be a continuous bijection, with X compact and Y Hausdorff. Every closed subset C⊆X is compact. Its continuous image f(C) is compact, and every compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed. Hence f is a closed map. For every closed C⊆X,
(f−1)−1(C)=f(C)
(74)
is closed in Y, so f−1 is continuous. Therefore f is a homeomorphism. This is the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem.

Let p∈Rm be Player I's row-strategy distribution and let e denote an all-ones vector of the required dimension. Against column j, the expected payoff is (pTA)j​. Thus Player I's matrix-game optimization problem is
p,vmax​vsubject toATp≥ve,quadeTp=1,quadp≥0​.
(203)
Equivalently, Player I maximizes minj​(pTA)j​ over the probability simplex.
Let q∗ be an optimal mixed strategy for Player II and let the game value be v∗. A sufficient condition for a probability vector p to be optimal for Player I is
pTA≥v∗eT​.
(204)
Indeed, this makes p guarantee at least v∗ against every pure column and hence every mixed strategy. On the other hand, the optimality of q∗ prevents any row strategy from obtaining more than v∗ against q∗. Therefore p is optimal. This is the mixed-strategy optimality certificate for a matrix game.
Now suppose that A is invertible and symmetric and that A−1e≥0. Put
c=eTA−1e,p=q=cA−1e​.
(205)
The vector A−1e is nonzero and nonnegative, so c>0 and p,q are probability vectors. Since A is symmetric,
pTA=ceT​,Aq=ce​.
(206)
Thus p guarantees 1/c and q holds the payoff to 1/c. By the minimax theorem,
v∗=eTA−1e1​​.
(207)
This proves the symmetric inverse formula for a matrix-game equilibrium.
For the card game, the payoff matrix to Player I is
A=​234​34−5​4−5−6​​.
(208)
It is symmetric and invertible, and direct solution of Ax=e gives
A−1e=1141​​4145​​,eTA−1e=5725​.
(209)
The preceding result therefore gives the same optimal strategy for both players:
p∗=q∗=​41/502/251/10​​​.
(210)
Thus each player chooses cards 1,2,3 with probabilities 41/50,2/25,1/10, respectively, and the value to Player I is
v∗=2557​ pounds​.
(211)
This is the three-card threshold-sum zero-sum game.
